why_this_tool: MCP is the open standard the lesson teaches, so building a server against its own documentation practises the contract of tools, resources, prompts, lifecycle and authorization that every compliant host understands.
alternatives: Framework-specific tool definitions such as LangChain or LlamaIndex tools (quick to write but tied to one agent framework), plain function calling against an OpenAPI-described REST API (reuses existing APIs but has no shared discovery or lifecycle), and agent-to-agent protocols such as A2A (connect whole agents to each other, not systems to one agent).

setup.why: Every later step uses one SDK's way of declaring tools, resources and prompts. Choosing once keeps the path consistent.

steps.why: This is the core of building a server with an SDK. The SDK turns your function signature and description into the tool definition a model reads.

steps.do: Run the server over the stdio transport and keep everything except protocol messages off standard output.
steps.done_when: The process starts without an error and stays running, waiting for input, with nothing printed to standard output.

source.title: Build an MCP server - Model Context Protocol

steps.why: A first run proves the server starts and waits for a client. On stdio, any stray print corrupts the JSON-RPC stream.

steps.do: Read the participants section and label the host, the client and the server in your own setup.
steps.done_when: You can say which process on your laptop is the host, which is the client and which is the server.
steps.why: The trust boundary of a deployment follows these three roles. One host runs one client per server, which is why servers stay isolated from each other.

steps.do: Write out by hand the initialize request, the initialize response and the initialized notification that your server would exchange with a client.
steps.done_when: Your three JSON-RPC messages carry a protocol version, the capabilities of each side and the correct method names, matching the section.
steps.why: The lifecycle begins with version and capability negotiation. Knowing these three messages lets you diagnose a connection that never reaches the operation phase.

steps.do: Create a resource on your server that exposes read-only data by URI, plus one resource template with a parameter.
steps.done_when: The server declares one fixed resource and one templated resource, each with a URI, a name and a content type.

steps.why: Resources are context the application chooses to attach, not actions the model takes. Separating them from tools keeps the contract clear.

steps.do: Create a prompt on your server that takes one argument and returns a reusable message template for a common workflow.
steps.done_when: The server declares a named prompt with a described argument that returns at least one message.

source.title: Understanding MCP servers - Model Context Protocol

steps.why: Prompts are the user-controlled primitive. They let a customer's team ship a vetted way of invoking your tools and resources.

steps.do: Write a failing case for your tool and return it as a tool execution error, as distinct from a protocol error.
steps.done_when: Calling the tool with bad input yields a result flagged as an error with a readable message, and the server keeps running.
steps.why: A model can recover from an execution error it can read, but not from a broken protocol exchange. This distinction shapes how agents behave on bad input.

steps.do: Write a small client that launches your server over stdio, initializes a session and lists its tools; save the listing, add a tool, then compare a second listing against it. Skip the chat loop, which needs a paid model API key.
steps.done_when: The client prints your tool names, and the second saved listing differs from the first only by the tool you added.

steps.why: A saved capability listing is the server's contract in a form you can compare. Diffing it between versions shows exactly what changed for every host.

steps.do: Configure Claude Desktop to launch your server by registering its command and absolute path in the host's server configuration.
steps.done_when: After a restart the host lists your server's tools, and a tool call you approve returns a result in the conversation.

steps.why: Registering the server with a host is how it gets handed to users. It also shows how the host presents your tools and asks for approval.

source.title: Build with Agent Skills - Model Context Protocol

steps.why: The transport decides who runs the server, where credentials live and whether authorization is required. That is the main deployment decision for a customer.

steps.do: Reproduce a startup failure by breaking the configured server path, find the cause in the host's logs, then restore the path.
steps.done_when: You can point to the log line that shows the failed launch, and the server connects again once the path is restored.
steps.why: Most field problems are launch and environment problems. A repeatable way to read the logs turns a silent failure into a short fix.

steps.do: Write the authorization plan for an HTTP version of your server, covering the authorization server, the resource identifier used as token audience and the rule for rejecting tokens issued for another resource. A real deployment needs a hosted authorization server; a local one in a container is the closest substitute.
steps.done_when: Your one-page plan names the audience value your server validates and states that it never forwards a client's token to an upstream service.
steps.why: A remote server is a protected resource that must accept only tokens issued for it. Passing a client's token through to other services creates a confused deputy.
